title: 9 Easy Morning Exercises for Seniors at Home (Thanksgiving Weekend and Every Day)
summary: Discover 9 easy morning exercises for seniors at home to improve strength, balance, and mobility. Build a simple daily routine with no special equipment needed.
body_markdown:
The best morning exercises at home are the ones you'll actually do before the coffee gets cold. For most older adults that means a seated warm-up, some light strength work, a short morning walk, and an optional walk after dinner, with a sturdy chair and nothing to buy. The nine moves below cover the three things the[CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/physical-activity-basics/guidelines/older-adults.html) says adults 65 and older need every week: aerobic activity, muscle strengthening, and balance. They also happen to be the moves that make Thanksgiving weekend easier, from the long drive to the long sit at the table.


GoGoGrandparent is the phone service that gets older adults where they need to go, and we run online fitness classes for members too. So we see what a routine like this does for the members who keep it: the ride to the walking group every Tuesday, the class joined from the kitchen, the appointment they walk into on their own. Call 1 (855) 464-6872 if a ride, a grocery order or a class would help with any of it.


## **Why do a morning routine instead of "exercising when I can"?**


Because the morning is the one part of the day nobody else has claimed yet. Appointments, visitors, the telephone, the weather and a holiday weekend all arrive later, and ten minutes completed at 8 a.m. is ten minutes you have already banked.


There's a second reason. Stiffness is at its worst first thing in the morning. Joints that sat still for eight hours loosen with slow movement, and the day's first stairs, first car door and first grocery bag go better when the ankles, hips and shoulders have already warmed up. The[National Institute on Aging](https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/exercise-and-physical-activity/three-types-exercise-can-improve-your-health-and-physical) puts it plainly: muscle-strengthening work "can help you stay independent and make it easier to perform everyday activities, such as getting up from a chair, climbing stairs, and carrying groceries."


That is the whole point of a morning routine: not a smaller waist, but a bigger life, and more years of managing it independently.


## **What do you need before you start?**


- **A sturdy chair without wheels** , back against a wall if you have any balance worries.
- **Shoes with a grip** , not slippers, even indoors.
- **Water** within reach, because most people have not had a glass since the night before.
- **Your doctor's okay** if you've had surgery, a fall, a heart event or new pain in the last few months. Bring the nine moves below to your next appointment and ask which ones to skip.
- **A phone nearby** , not for the workout but for the same reason you'd carry one on a walk.


If you're already breathing hard, feeling dizzy, or something hurts in a sharp way rather than a working way, stop. Easy means easy.


## **The 9 easy morning exercises, in order**


Do them in this order, because it runs from gentle to a little more demanding and from sitting to standing, so the body warms up the way it should.


### **1. Deep breathing, before your feet hit the floor**


Sit on the edge of the bed or in your chair. Breathe in slowly through the nose for a count of four, hold for two, and let it out through the mouth for a count of six, and repeat the cycle for five rounds.


This is belly breathing, sometimes called diaphragmatic breathing, and it does two jobs. It wakes up the lungs after a night of shallow breathing, and it settles the morning rush before it starts. If you tend to stand up too fast and feel light-headed, this minute of sitting is also your safety margin.


### **2. Ankle circles**


Still seated, lift one foot an inch off the floor. Draw ten slow circles with your big toe in one direction, then ten the other way, and then switch feet and repeat.


Ankles are the first joint to stiffen and the last one most people think about. Loosening them first thing makes the first stairs and the first curb of the day steadier. In a chair class you'll hear these called ankle rotations.


### **3. Seated marches**


Sit tall, hands resting on your thighs or holding the sides of the chair. Lift one knee a few inches, lower it, then the other. Keep going for one minute. Swing the arms gently if you'd like.


Seated marching, as a chair class would call it, is your warm-up for everything below. It raises the heart rate a little, gets blood moving in the legs after a night in bed, and, on a rainy morning, it's a perfectly good stand-in for the first part of a walk. If you watch the morning news, march through one story and rest through the next.


### **4. Seated leg lifts**


Straighten one leg out in front of you until the knee is as straight as it comfortably goes. Hold for three seconds, lower slowly, and repeat ten times on each side before moving on.


Physical therapists call these seated knee extensions, and that hold is the thigh muscle doing the exact work it does when you rise from a chair or climb a step. Strength here is what keeps "I'll get up in a minute" from becoming "can someone give me a hand." Add a second set after a week or two.


### **5. Arm circles and shoulder rolls**


Sit or stand. Roll both shoulders backward five times, then forward five times. Then hold your arms out to the sides, a little below shoulder height, and make small circles for twenty seconds, then reverse.


Shoulders carry the day's tension and the day's bags. Loosening them first thing makes reaching the top shelf, fastening a seat belt and lifting a roasting pan less of a negotiation. If your arms tire before twenty seconds, rest them on the chair arms and circle from the elbows instead.


### **6. A chair yoga stretch for the back and hips**


Sit toward the front of the chair, feet flat. Put your right hand on the outside of your left knee and your left hand on the back of the chair. Breathe in and sit tall. Breathe out and turn gently to the left, looking over your shoulder. Hold for three breaths, come back to center, and do the other side.


The twist is a seated spinal twist. Then a hip stretch some classes call the figure-four: cross your right ankle over your left knee, sit tall, and lean forward a little until you feel it in the right hip, hold for three breaths, and switch sides. Skip this one if you've had a hip replacement and your surgeon hasn't cleared it.


Chair yoga is the class many people try first, because nothing in it asks you to get down on the floor. Our guide to[seated exercises for seniors](https://www.gogograndparent.com/blog/9-seated-exercises-to-boost-physical-health) has a longer chair routine for days when standing isn't on the menu.


### **7. Bicep curls, chair rises and a one-leg stand**


Sit tall in your chair with a can of beans or a full water bottle in one hand, elbow tucked at your side. Curl the can up toward your shoulder and lower it slowly, ten times, then switch hands and repeat. This is a bicep curl, and the can is the right weight for most beginners. Make it heavier only when ten repetitions have felt easy for a couple of weeks.


Then the chair rise, which some people know as the sit-to-stand. Scoot to the front of a sturdy chair, feet flat and a little apart. Lean forward slightly, stand up using your legs, with your hands on your thighs or the chair arms only if you need them, and sit back down slowly. Ten times.


For balance, stand behind the chair and hold the back with both hands. Lift one foot an inch off the floor and stand on the other leg for ten seconds, then switch. Standing on one leg is one of the balance activities the CDC names for adults 65 and older.


The CDC guideline for adults 65 and older is muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days a week plus balance activities, and these three count. The chair rise is the single most useful strength exercise an older adult can do, because it is the movement itself, practiced. Every rise from a dining chair, a car seat or the edge of the bed draws on the same thighs and the same balance, and practicing it ten times in a quiet kitchen is considerably easier than discovering a weakness in a crowded restaurant.


### **8. A short morning walk**


Out the door, to the corner or around the block, and back. Ten minutes is a good start. The CDC's example for the week is 30 minutes a day on five days, and a morning walk is the easiest place for that to grow. On icy or wet mornings, walk the hallway or the length of the house a few times instead.


Walking is the aerobic part of the week, and it adds up: the CDC's target for adults 65 and older is at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, which the CDC says could be 30 minutes a day, five days a week. A morning walk also does what no indoor move does. It gets you daylight, air, and a neighbor to wave at.


How hard should the walk feel? The CDC describes moderate intensity as a 5 or 6 on a scale where sitting is 0 and your hardest effort is 10, and offers a simpler measurement: at a moderate pace you can still talk, but you could not sing the words to a favorite song. If conversation is comfortable and singing is not, the pace is right. If you cannot get a sentence out, slow down, and if you could perform the whole chorus, pick it up a little.


If walking alone isn't something you want to do, that's reasonable, and it has an answer. Many senior centers, parks departments and churches run morning walking groups.[GoGo Rides](https://www.gogograndparent.com/services/rides-for-seniors) gets you there by phone: call 1 (855) 464-6872, and an operator books an Uber or Lyft with a driver vetted for high ratings, while the GoGo Guardians team is able to monitor the trip. Call again when the group is done and you'd like to head home.


### **9. The after-meal walk**


This one isn't for the morning, and on Thanksgiving it's the most important of the nine. After the big meal, before the pie, take a slow walk around the block with whoever will come. Fifteen minutes is plenty, and a slow pace is the point.


A slow walk after the meal is the easiest way to get the whole table outside and talking, and it turns the longest sit of the year into two shorter ones, which your hips and your back will thank you for on Friday morning.


## **How do these nine fit into Thanksgiving weekend?**


Thanksgiving falls on Thursday, November 26 this year, and the weekend around it is four days of driving, sitting, eating and standing in a kitchen. Last year[AAA](https://newsroom.aaa.com/2025/11/aaa-thanksgiving-travel-forecast-2025/) expected 81.8 million Americans to travel for the holiday, 73 million of them by car, which means a great many older adults spent the better part of a day folded into a passenger seat. The routine bends to fit all of it:


- **Thursday morning:** the full routine, numbers 1 through 8, before anyone arrives or before you leave. It's the only quiet window you'll get.
- **Before you get in the car:** ankle circles and seated marches. A long ride goes better on legs that have moved.
- **At the table:** nobody will notice ankle circles under the tablecloth. Stand up between courses.
- **After dinner:** the walk. Invite the grandchildren. They have energy to burn and you have stories to tell.
- **Friday morning:** the routine again, gently. Shorter holds, fewer repetitions. The point is to loosen Thursday out of your back.
- **In the kitchen:** shoulder rolls between tasks. Bending over a hot stove and chopping for an hour is where holiday neck and shoulder pain comes from.


One more holiday tip that has nothing to do with exercise. If carrying groceries is the hard part of the week, GoGo Grocery can bring the heavy bags to the door. Same phone number, press 7 for delivery, and an operator takes the list.


## **What if you'd rather follow along with a class?**


Some people do better with a voice telling them what comes next. GoGoGrandparent's[Grow with GoGo](https://www.gogograndparent.com/services/grow-with-gogo) program runs weekly chair yoga and functional fitness classes online, joined from home and included with a GoGo membership. The instructors build every class for seniors and people with disabilities, with seated options throughout. Past classes are on[GoGoGrandparent's YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/@gogograndparent) , so a morning routine can be a class video with a teacher instead of a list on a screen.


And if the class you'd rather join is in person, at a senior center or a community pool, that is a ride we book every day.


## **How do you make a morning routine stick?**


The seated part of the routine takes a few minutes and the walk a few more, and the exercises themselves are not the hard part. The hard part is day nine, when it's raining, the coffee is already poured and nobody would know if you skipped it. A few things that help:


- **Tie it to something you already do.** After the first cup of coffee. Before the morning paper. The routine borrows the habit's momentum.
- **Keep the chair where you can see it.** A chair against the wall by the window is an invitation. A yoga mat rolled up in the closet is a chore.
- **Count days, not reps.** A calendar on the fridge and a check mark. Ten check marks in a row is a surprisingly good feeling.
- **Do less rather than nothing.** On a bad morning, do the breathing and the ankle circles and call it done. The streak survives.
- **Tell someone.** A daughter who asks "did you do your marches?" on the Sunday call is worth more than any app.


Falls are the reason this matters more than it sounds. The CDC reports that more than one out of four people 65 and older falls each year, and falling once doubles the chances of falling again. The CDC's answer is the mix above: muscle-strengthening and balance activities every week, which is what the leg lifts, the chair rises and the one-leg stand are. None of the nine moves is dramatic. Done most mornings, together, they add up.


## **Nine moves, one chair, every morning**


Belly breathing, ankle circles, seated marching, leg lifts, shoulder rolls, a chair stretch, curls and chair rises, a walk, and a second walk after the big meal. That is the whole program, and it needs nothing more than a chair, a pair of shoes and the first quiet stretch of the day.


GoGoGrandparent has helped older adults get to classes, appointments and walking groups since 2016, and bring the groceries home afterward. Whatever part of staying active needs a ride, a delivery or a class, it's one phone call: 1 (855) 464-6872.


## **FAQ**


### **What are the best morning exercises for seniors at home?**


A short seated warm-up (belly breathing, ankle circles, seated marching, seated knee extensions, shoulder rolls), a gentle chair stretch, a few minutes of strength and balance work (bicep curls with a can, chair rises, a one-leg stand), and a short walk. Together they cover the aerobic, strength and balance activity the CDC recommends for adults 65 and older.


### **How long should a senior's morning routine take?**


The seated warm-up takes a few minutes, the strength and balance work a few more, and the walk is the longest part: start with ten minutes and let it grow toward the CDC's 30 minutes a day. A short routine you keep beats a long one you drop.


### **Can I do these exercises if I use a walker or a cane?**


Ask your physical therapist which moves and supports fit you, and start with the seated options they recommend. Exercises 1 through 6 are seated or done holding a chair. Skip anything that causes sharp pain.


### **Is it safe to exercise after a big Thanksgiving meal?**


A slow walk after dinner is fine for most people and a good way to get everyone outside. Save anything more energetic for the next morning. If you have a heart condition or diabetes, ask your doctor what's right for you.
